newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian socialists see cabinet despite protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian socialists see cabinet despite protests.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists will form a new government next week despite 27 days of opposition protests to demand immediate elections, Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov said on Saturday.
He said that Nikolai Dobrev, nominated to form the new government, would be prime minister if the cabinet wins the approval of the 240-seat parliament.
"I'm sure next week Bulgaria will have a new government but it is hard to predict what the future of this government will be," Parvanov said in an interview with state television.

Students and the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) have vowed to intensify their protests, and disrupt road and rail links further, if the Socialists form a new government instead of opting for immediate elections.
Bulgaria has had a caretaker cabinet, unable to act on a deep economic crisis, since December when prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned.
Parvanov said the Socialists could count on 122 votes in parliament, less than their 125 seats but an absolute majority and able to win the required confidence vote.

He said he was willing to support an all-party coalition government with the active participation of President Petar Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal who handed the Socialists a crushing election defeat last November.
But Parvanov said it was unlikely the opposition would accept such a solution to end Bulgaria's political and economic crisis and, therefore, the Socialists would form a cabinet of their own.

"I think that the anti-crisis programme which is proposed by Nikolai Dobrev is quite constructive but will still need about 30 to 40 days to implement and to regain the confidence of the people," Parvanov said.
He said Bulgaria must have a government immediately to pass legislation to stop the collapse of the lev and inflation at 50 percent a month. The government must also pass the 1997 budget.
The Socialists have said they would hold general elections, due in December 1998, later this year but this offer has failed to satisfy the opposition, who want the vote held immediately.
Thousands of festive protesters streamed through central Sofia on Saturday on the 27th day of anti-government rallies.
"We think that victory is very close," opposition leader Ivan Kostov told an enthusiastic and cheering throng from the steps of the Alexander Nevski Orthodox cathedral.
Bulgarians from all walks of life poured into the cathedral square to hear popular bands and singers bang out tunes and opposition leaders whip up support.
"Communists can't jump," shouted one speaker and the mass of people, including Kostov, began to leap up and down.
University students earlier marched through Sofia, taking over key intersections and halting traffic.
Several thousand opposition supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fourth day. The UDF said it would reinforce the blockades and offered free rides from Sofia.

About 100 riot police stood nearby while tyres burned in the highway at Doupnitsa 60 kms (35 miles) south of Sofia. Pop music blared, protesters pinned red carnations on police and a festive mood prevailed despite the cold.
Kostov warned the Socialists that similar disruptions would erupt across Bulgaria next week if they voted in a new cabinet instead of calling elections.
"The Socialists should consider this an example of what will happen if they pass a government through parliament," he said. "The Doupnitsa road and rail blockades will become nationwide actions."
